steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting Xiezhi, an ever-updating benchmark for evaluating the domain knowledge of large language models. Motivate why existing benchmarks are not enough, describe what Xiezhi contains and our evaluation setting, and summarize the experiments and findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Domain knowledge and recent LLMs
- Benchmarks lag behind LLM capabilities
- Three needs a benchmark for LLMs should meet
- Xiezhi: composition and construction
- New evaluation setting
- Experiments and findings

steps.name: detailed_outline

  - (3) go ahead of training set (cite): larger corpora; new benchmarks enter training data sooner; benchmarks must be fresher than training data
- Xiezhi
  - comprehensive, multi-disciplinary, auto-updating; named after mythical creature (fairness, judgement)
  - 249587 questions, 516 disciplines, 13 categories: philosophy, economics, law, education, literature, history, natural sciences, engineering, agriculture, medicine, military science, management, arts
  - disciplines from Chinese Disciplinary Taxonomy (Chinese Ministry of Education)
  - Xiezhi-Meta: 20,124 manually selected/annotated questions from Chinese Graduate Entrance Examination
  - annotation model trained on Xiezhi-Meta -> labels 170k exam MCQs + 80k MCQs auto-generated from academic surveys
  - Xiezhi-Specialty (14,041) and Xiezhi-Interdiscipline (10,746), Chinese and English; balanced, less sensitive, less China-centric

  - 50 options per question vs 4 -> lower random-guess accuracy

  - 47 LLMs, four benchmarks, 0-shot / 1-shot / 3-shot, Chinese and English Xiezhi

  - humans still far better in economics, jurisprudence, pedagogy, literature, history, management

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Domain knowledge means an in-depth comprehension of the world, and it requires various cognitive skills to be developed, like memorization, abstraction, logical thinking, reasoning, and imagination. For a long time humans have shown unparalleled proficiency in domain knowledge, far beyond any machine learning model. But recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), including Bloom, Llama, ChatGLM, GPT4 and many other models, have shown remarkable capabilities in domain text understanding. So it is time to propose more comprehensive and more prospective evaluations than before, to find out whether LLMs have actually acquired knowledge or have just acquired a better imitation ability.

Building benchmarks is crucial for automatic evaluation, since benchmarks make it possible to compare models efficiently, systematically and at scale. However, as LLMs keep growing in size and complexity, they show outstanding performance on a wide range of domain-specific tasks. Because of this even newly released benchmarks like MMLU, BIG-bench or HELM all fall behind the capabilities of LLMs quickly.

Looking at the performance of LLMs, we think a benchmark for evaluating LLMs should meet the following needs. (1) It needs to cover more tasks. Cutting-edge LLMs have put multiple capabilities into unified Text-to-Text transformer models, so the evaluation of LLMs should look at abilities in multiple tasks. (2) It needs to show the differences between LLMs. Because of the emergent capacity of the models, it is likely that SoTA LLMs, by learning knowledge in different domains, now have some level of performance in all domains. To accurately evaluate the differences between LLMs with different capacities, the benchmark should break down the evaluation dimensions into more detailed categories. This allows a more precise assessment of each model's capabilities and gives useful insights into their relative strengths and weaknesses. (3) It needs to go ahead of the training set. LLMs are trained on more and more extensive corpora, so newly released benchmarks may become part of the LLMs' training data much sooner than before. A prerequisite for effective evaluation is that the benchmarks are fresher than the training data used by LLMs.

- Xiezhi: comprehensive, multi-disciplinary, auto-updating; named after mythical creature (fairness, judgement)
  - 249587 questions, 516 disciplines, 13 categories (philosophy ... arts)
  - disciplines from Chinese Disciplinary Taxonomy (Chinese Ministry of Education)
  - Xiezhi-Meta: 20,124 annotated questions from Chinese Graduate Entrance Examination -> trains annotation model
  - annotation model labels 170k exam MCQs + 80k MCQs generated from academic surveys
  - Xiezhi-Specialty (14,041) / Xiezhi-Interdiscipline (10,746), Chinese + English; single vs multiple domains
- Evaluation setting: 50 options instead of 4; rank options by generation probability instead of instructions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Domain knowledge means an in-depth comprehension of the world, and it requires various cognitive skills to be developed, like memorization, abstraction, logical thinking, reasoning, and imagination. For a long time humans have shown unparalleled proficiency in domain knowledge, far beyond any machine learning model. But recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), including Bloom, Llama, ChatGLM, GPT4 and many other models, have shown remarkable capabilities in domain text understanding. So it is time to propose more comprehensive and more prospective evaluations than before, to find out whether LLMs have actually acquired knowledge or have just acquired a better imitation ability.

Building benchmarks is crucial for automatic evaluation, since benchmarks make it possible to compare models efficiently, systematically and at scale. However, as LLMs keep growing in size and complexity, they show outstanding performance on a wide range of domain-specific tasks. Because of this even newly released benchmarks like MMLU, BIG-bench or HELM all fall behind the capabilities of LLMs quickly.

Looking at the performance of LLMs, we think a benchmark for evaluating LLMs should meet the following needs. (1) It needs to cover more tasks. Cutting-edge LLMs have put multiple capabilities into unified Text-to-Text transformer models, so the evaluation of LLMs should look at abilities in multiple tasks. (2) It needs to show the differences between LLMs. Because of the emergent capacity of the models, it is likely that SoTA LLMs, by learning knowledge in different domains, now have some level of performance in all domains. To accurately evaluate the differences between LLMs with different capacities, the benchmark should break down the evaluation dimensions into more detailed categories. This allows a more precise assessment of each model's capabilities and gives useful insights into their relative strengths and weaknesses. (3) It needs to go ahead of the training set. LLMs are trained on more and more extensive corpora, so newly released benchmarks may become part of the LLMs' training data much sooner than before. A prerequisite for effective evaluation is that the benchmarks are fresher than the training data used by LLMs.

Based on these needs, we propose a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary, auto-updating benchmark for domain knowledge evaluation. We call it Xiezhi, after a mythical creature that symbolizes fairness and judgement. Xiezhi has 249587 questions with 516 disciplines, from 13 different categories: philosophy, economics, law, education, literature, history, natural sciences, engineering, agriculture, medicine, military science, management, and arts. The 516 disciplines come from the Chinese Disciplinary Taxonomy, which is a comprehensive hierarchical classification system of domain knowledge proposed by the Chinese Ministry of Education and widely acknowledged in China. We manually selected and annotated 20,124 questions from the Chinese Graduate Entrance Examination that cover these 516 labels, and these form the Xiezhi-Meta dataset. Xiezhi-Meta is used to train an annotation model that can estimate the relevance between questions and disciplinary labels. Then the annotation model tags disciplinary labels to 170k multiple-choice questions that come from diverse examinations, and also to 80k multiple-choice questions auto-generated from academic surveys. To make Xiezhi easier to use and to follow the inclination that "consolidate increasing capabilities into single LLMs", we also present Xiezhi-Specialty and Xiezhi-Interdiscipline, in both Chinese and English versions, with 14,041 and 10,746 questions respectively that are more balanced, less sensitive, and less China-centric. Xiezhi-Specialty has questions that can be solved with knowledge from a single domain, and Xiezhi-Interdiscipline has questions that need knowledge from multiple domains to solve.

We also propose a new evaluation setting in this paper to get more precise evaluation results. We use 50 options for each multiple-choice question, whereas previous researchers use only 4 options, so the accuracy of random guessing is much lower and the model's real capabilities are better revealed. We also rank all options of each model by generation probability, whereas previous researchers use instructions to ask each model for its choice. This avoids inaccurate evaluations caused by the model being unable to answer multiple-choice questions or by errors when extracting the generated content.

To give a detailed analysis of the current development status of LLMs, and to show the effectiveness of the Xiezhi Benchmark and our evaluation process, we run experiments on 47 famous LLMs on four benchmarks from different works in our evaluation setting. The experiments use 0-shot, 1-shot and 3-shot demonstration settings, which means using a small number of examples to show how to solve a question, and all LLMs are evaluated on both the Chinese and English versions of Xiezhi. This lets us analyze the LLM results based on their best performance. The results show that the best-performing LLMs, when tested with multiple-choice questions, have gone beyond the level of average practitioners in science, engineering, agronomy, and medicine. But humans still greatly outperform all LLMs in economics, jurisprudence, pedagogy, literature, history, and management. We also looked at the differences in performance of various LLMs across different benchmarks. Compared to existing knowledge evaluation benchmarks, Xiezhi covers the broadest range of domains, has the most questions, and has the most current data. Our experiments show that because of the huge diversity of knowledge domains in Xiezhi and its fifty-to-one evaluation method, even marginal improvements in any aspect of a model can be accurately assessed. So it is the best at telling apart the capability differences among various LMs, from GPT-4 down to LLMs with only 560M parameters. Therefore it is the most appropriate benchmark for evaluating LLMs of differing competencies.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Domain knowledge encompasses an in-depth comprehension of the world, which requires the cultivation of various cognitive skills, such as memorization, abstraction, logical thinking, reasoning, and imagination. For a long time, humans have exhibited unparalleled proficiency in domain knowledge, far exceeding any machine learning model. Nevertheless, recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs), including Bloom [1], Llama [2], ChatGLM [3], GPT4 [4,5] and many other models, have shown remarkable capabilities in domain text understanding [6]. It is time to propose more comprehensive and more prospective evaluations than before, to explore whether LLMs have actually acquired knowledge or just a better imitation ability [7].

Constructing benchmarks is crucial for automatic evaluation, as benchmarks facilitate efficient, systematic, and scalable comparisons among models. However, as LLMs continue to grow in size and complexity, they exhibit outstanding performance across a wide range of domain-specific tasks. As a result, even newly released benchmarks like MMLU [8], BIG-bench [7] or HELM [9] quickly lag behind the capabilities of LLMs [10].

Considering LLMs' performance, we conclude that a benchmark used to evaluate LLMs should meet the following needs: (1) Needs to cover more tasks [7]: Cutting-edge LLMs have integrated multiple capabilities into unified Text-to-Text transformer models [11], so the evaluation of LLMs should focus on abilities in multiple tasks. (2) Needs to manifest the disparities among LLMs [12]: Considering the emergent capacity of the models [6], it is likely that SoTA LLMs, by learning knowledge in different domains, now have a certain level of performance in all domains. To accurately evaluate the distinctions between LLMs with varying capacities, the benchmark should break the evaluation dimensions down into more detailed categories. This allows a more precise assessment of each model's capabilities and provides valuable insights into their relative strengths and weaknesses. (3) Needs to go ahead of the training set [5]: As LLMs are trained on increasingly extensive corpora, newly released benchmarks may become part of their training data much sooner than before. A prerequisite for effective evaluation is therefore to ensure that benchmarks are fresher than the training data used by LLMs.

In light of these needs, we propose a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary, auto-updating benchmark for domain knowledge evaluation, which we call Xiezhi, named after a mythical creature that symbolizes fairness and judgement. Xiezhi consists of 249587 questions with 516 disciplines, ranging over 13 different categories: philosophy, economics, law, education, literature, history, natural sciences, engineering, agriculture, medicine, military science, management, and arts. These 516 disciplines are derived from the Chinese Disciplinary Taxonomy, a comprehensive hierarchical classification system of domain knowledge proposed by the Chinese Ministry of Education and widely acknowledged in China. We manually selected and annotated 20,124 questions from the Chinese Graduate Entrance Examination covering these 516 labels to form the Xiezhi-Meta dataset. Xiezhi-Meta is used to train an annotation model capable of estimating the relevance between questions and disciplinary labels. The annotation model then tags disciplinary labels to 170k multiple-choice questions originating from diverse examinations, along with 80k multiple-choice questions auto-generated from academic surveys. To facilitate the usage of Xiezhi and align with the inclination to "consolidate increasing capabilities into single LLMs", we also present Xiezhi-Specialty and Xiezhi-Interdiscipline in both Chinese and English versions, consisting of 14,041 and 10,746 more balanced, less sensitive, and less China-centric questions respectively. Xiezhi-Specialty contains questions solvable with knowledge from a single domain, while Xiezhi-Interdiscipline contains questions that require knowledge from multiple domains.

To give more precise evaluation results, we propose a new evaluation setting in this paper. We set 50 options for each multiple-choice question, whereas previous researchers use only 4 options, which significantly reduces the accuracy of random guessing and thus better reveals the model's real capabilities. We rank all options of each model by generation probability, whereas previous researchers use instructions to query the choice made by each model, to avoid inaccurate evaluations caused by a model's inability to answer multiple-choice questions or by errors in extracting the generated content.

To provide a detailed analysis of the current development status of LLMs, and to demonstrate the effectiveness of the Xiezhi Benchmark and our proposed evaluation process, we conduct experiments on 47 famous LLMs across four benchmarks proposed in different works in our evaluation setting. The experiments are conducted in 0-shot, 1-shot and 3-shot demonstration settings, i.e. using a small number of examples to demonstrate how to solve a question, with all LLMs evaluated on both the Chinese and English versions of Xiezhi. This enables us to analyze the LLM results based on their optimal performance. Results show that the best-performing LLMs, when tested via multiple-choice questions, have surpassed the level of average practitioners in science, engineering, agronomy, and medicine. However, humans still greatly outperform all LLMs in economics, jurisprudence, pedagogy, literature, history, and management. We also examine the differences in performance of various LLMs across different benchmarks. Compared to existing knowledge evaluation benchmarks, Xiezhi covers the broadest range of domains, incorporates the largest number of questions, and consists of the most current data. As our experiments show, due to the vast diversity of knowledge domains covered in Xiezhi and its fifty-to-one evaluation method, even marginal improvements in any aspect of a model can be accurately assessed. It is thus most proficient in discerning the capability differences among various LMs, from GPT-4 to LLMs with only 560M parameters, and is consequently the most appropriate benchmark for evaluating LLMs of differing competencies.
